authoredSolutions.31: Match each monomer with the polymer it gives. Tetrafluoroethene \(CF_{2}=CF_{2}\) polymerises to polytetrafluoroethene, the commercial name of which is Teflon, so (A)-(III). Acrylonitrile \(CH_{2}=CH-CN\) gives polyacrylonitrile, sold as Orlon or Acrilan, so (B)-(I). Caprolactam is a cyclic amide (lactam) that undergoes ring-opening polymerisation to Nylon-6, so (C)-(IV). Isoprene (2-methylbuta-1,3-diene) is the repeating unit of natural rubber, which is cis-1,4-polyisoprene, so (D)-(II). The combination (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II) is option A.
authoredSolutions.32: The substrate is propene, \(CH_{3}-CH=CH_{2}\). Steps (i) \(B_{2}H_{6}\) and (ii) \(H_{2}O_{2}/NaOH\) together constitute hydroboration-oxidation, which adds water across the double bond with anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry, so the \(-OH\) lands on the terminal carbon and the product is propan-1-ol, \(CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}OH\). Step (iii) PCC is a mild oxidant that stops at the aldehyde stage, converting the primary alcohol into propanal, \(CH_{3}CH_{2}CHO\). Step (iv) \(CH_{3}MgBr\) adds a methyl group to the carbonyl carbon, and aqueous work-up gives the secondary alcohol butan-2-ol, \(CH_{3}CH_{2}CH(OH)CH_{3}\). That is the structure drawn in option A.
authoredSolutions.33: Photochemical (oxidising) smog requires abundant sunlight, warm temperature and a high load of \(NO_{x}\) and unburnt hydrocarbons from vehicular traffic, because the chain is initiated by the photodissociation \(NO_{2} \xrightarrow{h\nu} NO + O\), which then builds ozone, PAN and aldehydes. Among the four choices, Srinagar in January is a cold, high-latitude winter location with weak, low-angle sunlight, low ambient temperature and a comparatively small vehicular pollutant burden, so the photochemical chain is slowest there. Hence the possibility of photochemical smog is minimum in option D.
authoredSolutions.34: Calcination is the heating of an ore in the absence or limited supply of air, so that volatile matter such as water of hydration or carbon dioxide is expelled without any oxidation of the ore. Options A, B and C are all of this type: hydrated ferric oxide loses its water, and calcium carbonate and dolomite lose carbon dioxide, in each case giving the oxide. Option D, \(2PbS + 3O_{2} \rightarrow 2PbO + 2SO_{2}\), is the heating of a sulphide ore in an excess of air with genuine oxidation of sulphide to \(SO_{2}\); that is roasting, not calcination. Hence option D is the odd one out.
authoredSolutions.35: Take the statements one at a time. (A) is wrong: nitrogen in \(NF_{3}\) is \(sp^{3}\) hybridised with one lone pair, so the shape is trigonal pyramidal, not trigonal planar. (B) is right: \(N_{2}\) has a triple bond (bond order 3, bond length about \(110\) pm) while \(O_{2}\) has a double bond (bond order 2, bond length about \(121\) pm), so the \(N_{2}\) bond is shorter. (C) is right and is the standard molecular-orbital result: isoelectronic species fill the same MO diagram, so they have the same bond order, for example \(N_{2}\), \(CO\) and \(NO^{+}\) all have bond order 3. (D) is wrong: the dipole moment of water is about \(1.85\) D against roughly \(0.97\) D for \(H_{2}S\), because oxygen is far more electronegative than sulphur and the \(H-O-H\) angle is larger. Only (B) and (C) are correct, which is option D.
authoredSolutions.36: Aniline treated with \(NaNO_{2}\) (with mineral acid) at \(0-5\ ^{\circ}C\) is diazotised to benzenediazonium chloride, so intermediate A is \(C_{6}H_{5}N_{2}^{+}Cl^{-}\). A diazonium ion is a weak electrophile and therefore couples only with strongly activated rings. N,N-dimethylaniline carries the powerful electron-releasing \(-N(CH_{3})_{2}\) group, and coupling occurs at the position para to it, since the ortho positions are sterically hindered. Product B is therefore the azo dye \(C_{6}H_{5}-N=N-C_{6}H_{4}-N(CH_{3})_{2}\) (para), known as butter yellow. That azo structure with the \(-N=N-\) linkage is drawn in option B. Options A, C and D show hydrazine or biphenyl skeletons with \(N-N\) single bonds and are not coupling products.
authoredSolutions.37: Count the bridging oxygen atoms in each structure. Pyrophosphoric acid \(H_{4}P_{2}O_{7}\) is two \(PO_{4}\) tetrahedra sharing one corner, \((HO)_{2}(O)P-O-P(O)(OH)_{2}\), so it has exactly \(1\) \(P-O-P\) linkage. Trimetaphosphoric acid \((HPO_{3})_{3}\) is a six-membered cyclic ring of three \(PO_{4}\) tetrahedra, each pair joined by one bridging oxygen, giving \(3\) \(P-O-P\) linkages. \(P_{4}O_{10}\) has a tetrahedral \(P_{4}\) core in which each of the six \(P\cdots P\) edges carries one bridging oxygen, plus four terminal \(P=O\) bonds, so it has \(6\) \(P-O-P\) linkages. The sequence asked for is \(1, 3, 6\), which is option A.
authoredSolutions.38: Statement I is a postulate of the Bohr model: the angular momentum of the electron in a stationary state is restricted to \(mvr = n\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\), with \(n\) a positive integer, so it is quantised. Statement II is also correct and is the standard criticism of the model: a Bohr orbit assigns the electron a definite radius and a definite momentum simultaneously, whereas Heisenberg's principle requires \(\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \geq \dfrac{h}{4\pi}\), so such a sharply defined path cannot exist. Both statements are therefore correct, which is option A.
authoredSolutions.39: Reading the five structures: A is toluene (\(-CH_{3}\)), B is benzene, C is trifluoromethylbenzene (\(-CF_{3}\)), D is anisole (\(-OCH_{3}\)) and E is N,N-dimethylaniline (\(-N(CH_{3})_{2}\)). Electrophilic substitution is faster when the ring is more electron rich. The \(-N(CH_{3})_{2}\) group donates its nitrogen lone pair by resonance most strongly and is the best activator, so E is fastest. \(-OCH_{3}\) also donates by resonance but oxygen is more electronegative and holds its lone pair more tightly, so D comes next. \(-CH_{3}\) activates only weakly, by hyperconjugation and induction, so A follows. Benzene B is the unsubstituted reference. \(-CF_{3}\) has three fluorines exerting a powerful \(-I\) pull with no compensating donation, so C is strongly deactivated and slowest. The order is \(E > D > A > B > C\), which is option B.
authoredSolutions.40: Examine each claim. (A) is wrong: for \(1\times10^{-8}\) M HCl the acid contribution is comparable with the water autoionisation, so one must solve \([H^{+}]^{2} - 10^{-8}[H^{+}] - 10^{-14} = 0\), giving \([H^{+}] \approx 1.05\times10^{-7}\) M and \(pH \approx 6.98\). An acid can never give \(pH = 8\). (B) is correct: removing one proton from \(H_{2}PO_{4}^{-}\) leaves \(HPO_{4}^{2-}\), which is by definition its conjugate base. (C) is correct: autoionisation of water is endothermic, so by Le Chatelier's principle \(K_{w}\) rises as temperature rises, from \(10^{-14}\) at \(25\ ^{\circ}C\) to about \(5.5\times10^{-14}\) at \(50\ ^{\circ}C\). (D) is wrong: at half neutralisation \([HA] = [A^{-}]\), so the Henderson-Hasselbalch relation gives \(pH = pK_{a}\), not \(\tfrac{1}{2}pK_{a}\). Only (B) and (C) hold, which is option D.
authoredSolutions.41: Beryllium and magnesium salts do not impart any characteristic colour to a bunsen flame, unlike the salts of calcium, strontium and barium. The reason is exactly what (R) states: \(Be\) and \(Mg\) are small ions with very high effective nuclear charge, so their valence electrons are bound tightly and the excitation energy required is large, larger than the energy available in a bunsen flame. No electron is promoted, so no visible light is emitted on relaxation. Hence Assertion (A) is false while Reason (R) is true, which is option B.
authoredSolutions.42: The starting material is 4-nitrotoluene and the target is 2-bromo-4-chlorobenzoic acid, so the \(-CH_{3}\) must become \(-COOH\), the \(-NO_{2}\) must become \(-Cl\), and a \(-Br\) must be installed ortho to the methyl carbon. Order matters. First \(Br_{2}/Fe\): the methyl group directs ortho and para while the nitro group directs meta, and both influences point to the position ortho to \(-CH_{3}\) and meta to \(-NO_{2}\), so bromination lands exactly where it is needed. Next \(Fe/H^{+}\) reduces \(-NO_{2}\) to \(-NH_{2}\). Then HONO (nitrous acid) diazotises the amine, and \(CuCl\) replaces the diazonium group by chlorine in the Sandmeyer reaction. Only at the end is \(KMnO_{4}\) used, oxidising the side-chain methyl to \(-COOH\); doing this earlier would destroy the amine and the \(-COOH\) group would then misdirect the bromination to the meta position. This is the sequence in option C.
authoredSolutions.43: The substrate is indane-1,2,3-trione. Its central carbonyl at C-2 is flanked by two more carbonyl groups, whose strong \(-I\) and \(-R\) withdrawal makes that carbon exceptionally electrophilic, and the same flanking groups destabilise the \(C=O\) by placing adjacent positive centres in conflict. Water therefore adds across this middle carbonyl and, unusually for a ketone, the gem-diol hydrate is the stable isolable species. Product A is 2,2-dihydroxyindane-1,3-dione, which is ninhydrin, the standard reagent for detecting amino acids. Option D shows precisely this, with two \(-OH\) groups on the central carbon and the two ring-fused carbonyls intact. Options B and C place the diol or the ketone at the wrong carbons, and option A shows a mono-ketone diol.
authoredSolutions.44: Arginine, like all \(\alpha\)-amino acids, exists in the solid and in solution as a dipolar zwitterion, and being a basic amino acid it also carries a guanidinium side chain. The strong electrostatic attraction between these charges makes it a crystalline solid (A is true) with a high melting or decomposition point (C is true), and the several ionisable groups (the \(-COOH\), the \(\alpha\)-\(NH_{3}^{+}\) and the guanidinium) give it more than one \(pK_{a}\) (B is true). Precisely because it is ionic, it dissolves well in water but is essentially insoluble in a non-polar solvent such as benzene. Hence (D) is the statement that is not true.
authoredSolutions.45: The water-gas shift reaction is \(CO + H_{2}O \xrightarrow{catalyst} CO_{2} + H_{2}\), carried out over an iron chromate catalyst at about \(673\) K to enrich water gas in dihydrogen. Carbon changes from \(+2\) in \(CO\) to \(+4\) in \(CO_{2}\), so carbon monoxide is oxidised to carbon dioxide, while hydrogen in water goes from \(+1\) to \(0\) and is reduced to \(H_{2}\). This matches option A. Option C reverses the direction, option B describes the earlier water-gas formation step, and option D is not a redox description at all.
authoredSolutions.46: The quality of Portland cement depends on the proportions of its raw oxides. For good quality cement the ratio of silica \(SiO_{2}\) to alumina \(Al_{2}O_{3}\) must lie between about \(2.5\) and \(4.0\), so the representative value is close to \(3\); alongside this, the ratio of lime \(CaO\) to the combined \(SiO_{2}\), \(Al_{2}O_{3}\) and \(Fe_{2}O_{3}\) must lie between \(2\) and \(3\). Too little lime makes the cement weak, too much makes it crumble. The value asked for is \(3\), option A.
authoredSolutions.47: Paper chromatography is a partition technique, not an adsorption technique. Chromatography paper is cellulose, which holds a considerable amount of moisture trapped in its pores, and it is this held water that acts as the stationary phase; the cellulose sheet itself is merely the inert support that carries it. The developing solvent that ascends the strip is the mobile phase, and components separate according to how they partition between the mobile solvent and the immobilised water. Hence option B is the correct description. Option A wrongly makes the paper absorb the mobile-phase water, while options C and D wrongly assign a stationary-phase role to the cellulose itself.
authoredSolutions.48: Chlorine on a benzene ring is deactivating through its strong \(-I\) effect, yet it is ortho and para directing because its lone pair can be delocalised into the ring, placing negative charge at the ortho and para carbons. Friedel-Crafts acylation of chlorobenzene with \(CH_{3}COCl/AlCl_{3}\) therefore substitutes at those positions, and the para product dominates because the bulky acylium electrophile, and the aluminium chloride complexed to it, are sterically hindered next to the chlorine. Because the ring is deactivated, substitution stops after one acyl group, so the di-acylated structures in options B and D are not formed, and option C places the acyl group meta. The major product is 4-chloroacetophenone, option A.
authoredSolutions.49: All four complexes are hexaaqua species of a \(+3\) metal ion, so the ligand and the charge are held constant and the splitting is decided by the metal ion itself. A more compact ion with a higher effective nuclear charge sits closer to the six donor oxygens and perturbs the \(d\) orbitals more strongly, raising \(\Delta_{0}\). Among \(Ti^{3+}\), \(Cr^{3+}\), \(Mn^{3+}\) and \(Fe^{3+}\), the \(Cr^{3+}\) ion (radius about \(0.615\) angstrom) is the smallest and has the most contracted \(3d^{3}\) set, giving the strongest metal-ligand interaction. This is also why \(Cr^{3+}\) with its \(t_{2g}^{3}\) configuration shows the largest crystal field stabilisation of the first transition series and is famously kinetically inert. Hence \([Cr(OH_{2})_{6}]^{3+}\), option A.
authoredSolutions.50: Caesium chloride crystallises in a body-centred cubic type of arrangement: \(Cl^{-}\) ions occupy the corners of the cube and a single \(Cs^{+}\) sits at the body centre, coordination number \(8:8\). The cation and anion touch along the body diagonal of the cube, and the body diagonal of a cube of edge \(a\) has length \(\sqrt{3}\,a\). That diagonal is made up of one anion radius at each end plus the full diameter of the central cation, that is \(2r_{Cl^{-}} + 2r_{Cs^{+}} = \sqrt{3}\,a\). Dividing by two gives \(r_{Cs^{+}} + r_{Cl^{-}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a\), which is option C. The relation \(\dfrac{a}{2}\) would apply to a rock-salt type edge contact and \(\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\) to a face-diagonal contact, neither of which holds here.
authoredSolutions.51: A homoleptic octahedral complex of \(Co^{2+}\) with water is \([Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}\). Cobalt in the \(+2\) state has the configuration \(3d^{7}\). Water is a weak field ligand, so \(\Delta_{0}\) is smaller than the pairing energy and the complex is high spin: the seven electrons fill as \(t_{2g}^{5}e_{g}^{2}\). The \(t_{2g}\) set holds three orbitals, and five electrons in three orbitals means two orbitals are doubly occupied and one carries a single electron. Hence the number of unpaired electrons in the \(t_{2g}\) set is \(1\). (The two \(e_{g}\) electrons are also unpaired, giving three unpaired electrons overall, but the question asks only about \(t_{2g}\).)
authoredSolutions.52: The complex is \([Cr(H_{2}O)_{5}Cl]Cl_{2}\). One chloride is bound inside the coordination sphere and is not precipitated by silver nitrate; the two chlorides outside the square brackets are the ionisable counter-ions and are the only ones available as free \(Cl^{-}\). Moles of complex \(= 20 \times 0.01 = 0.2\) mmol, so ionisable chloride \(= 2 \times 0.2 = 0.4\) mmol. Each mole of \(AgNO_{3}\) precipitates one mole of chloride, so \(0.4\) mmol of \(AgNO_{3}\) is needed. The volume is \(V = \dfrac{0.4}{0.1} = 4\) mL.
authoredSolutions.53: In acidic medium permanganate is reduced all the way to the manganous ion, the relevant half reaction being \(MnO_{4}^{-} + 8H^{+} + 5e^{-} \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_{2}O\), while iodide is oxidised to iodine, \(2I^{-} \rightarrow I_{2} + 2e^{-}\). Manganese in \(KMnO_{4}\) is in the \(+7\) state and finishes in the \(+2\) state, so the change in oxidation state is \(7 - 2 = 5\), which is also the number of electrons gained per manganese. The answer is \(5\).
authoredSolutions.54: Chromyl chloride is \(CrO_{2}Cl_{2}\), the red vapour produced when a chloride salt is warmed with potassium dichromate and concentrated sulphuric acid. Assign oxygen \(-2\) and chlorine \(-1\) and let the oxidation state of chromium be \(x\). For a neutral molecule, \(x + 2(-2) + 2(-1) = 0\), so \(x - 4 - 2 = 0\) and \(x = +6\). Chromium therefore retains the \(+6\) state it had in dichromate, which is consistent with the fact that the chromyl chloride test involves no redox change of chromium.
authoredSolutions.55: Isoelectronic species are those having the same total number of electrons. Count them one by one: \(O^{2-}\) has \(8 + 2 = 10\); \(F^{-}\) has \(9 + 1 = 10\); \(Al\) has \(13\); \(Mg^{2+}\) has \(12 - 2 = 10\); \(Na^{+}\) has \(11 - 1 = 10\); \(O^{+}\) has \(8 - 1 = 7\); \(Mg\) has \(12\); \(Al^{3+}\) has \(13 - 3 = 10\); \(F\) has \(9\). The species sharing the neon configuration of \(10\) electrons are \(O^{2-}\), \(F^{-}\), \(Mg^{2+}\), \(Na^{+}\) and \(Al^{3+}\), a total of \(5\). The remaining four each have a unique electron count, so they form no isoelectronic pair.
authoredSolutions.56: A \(30\%\ (w/v)\) solution contains \(30\) g of glucose in \(100\) mL of solution. With density \(1.2\) g cm\(^{-3}\), that \(100\) mL of solution weighs \(100 \times 1.2 = 120\) g, so the mass of water is \(120 - 30 = 90\) g. Moles of water \(= \dfrac{90}{18} = 5\) and moles of glucose \(= \dfrac{30}{180} = \dfrac{1}{6}\). Glucose is non-volatile, so Raoult's law gives \(p = x_{water}\,p^{\circ}\) with \(x_{water} = \dfrac{5}{5 + \tfrac{1}{6}} = \dfrac{5}{\tfrac{31}{6}} = \dfrac{30}{31}\). Hence \(p = 24 \times \dfrac{30}{31} = \dfrac{720}{31} = 23.2\) mmHg, which to the nearest integer is \(23\) mmHg.
authoredSolutions.57: The coagulating (or flocculation) value of an electrolyte is defined as the number of millimoles of that electrolyte needed to coagulate one litre of the sol. Here \(20\) mL of \(0.5\) M \(NaCl\) supplies \(20 \times 0.5 = 10\) millimoles, and this coagulates \(200\) mL of the \(As_{2}S_{3}\) sol. Scaling to one litre, the requirement is \(10 \times \dfrac{1000}{200} = 50\) millimoles per litre. The coagulating value of \(NaCl\) is therefore \(50\). (The sol is negatively charged, so it is the \(Na^{+}\) ion that does the coagulating, in line with the Hardy-Schulze rule.)
authoredSolutions.58: Since the concentrations are unchanged, equal rates mean equal rate constants, and the pre-exponential factor is taken to be the same. Equating the catalysed constant at \(300\) K with the uncatalysed one at \(600\) K, \(A e^{-E_{cat}/(R\cdot300)} = A e^{-300/(R\cdot600)}\) in kJ units, so \(\dfrac{E_{cat}}{300} = \dfrac{300}{600}\) and \(E_{cat} = 300 \times \dfrac{300}{600} = 150\) kJ mol\(^{-1}\) for the catalysed forward step. A catalyst lowers both barriers but cannot change the thermodynamics, so the enthalpy of reaction is still \(\Delta H = E_{a,forward} - E_{a,backward}\). Hence \(E_{a,backward} = 150 - 20 = 130\) kJ mol\(^{-1}\).
authoredSolutions.59: Test each statement. (A) is correct: conductivity is the conductance of a unit volume, and on dilution the number of current-carrying ions in that unit volume falls, so \(\kappa\) decreases for both strong and weak electrolytes. (B) is wrong, and states the opposite of (A): the number of ions per unit volume decreases, not increases, on dilution. (C) is correct: molar conductivity \(\Lambda_{m} = \dfrac{\kappa}{c}\), and \(\kappa\) falls more slowly than \(c\) because the total volume containing one mole increases, so \(\Lambda_{m}\) rises on dilution. (D) is correct: a strong electrolyte shows a small linear rise following \(\Lambda_{m} = \Lambda_{m}^{\circ} - A\sqrt{c}\), whereas a weak electrolyte shows a steep rise near infinite dilution, so the behaviour is genuinely different. (E) is wrong: for a weak electrolyte the change comes from an increase in the degree of dissociation on dilution, not a decrease. Three statements, (A), (C) and (D), are correct.
authoredSolutions.60: At the melting point the solid and the liquid are in equilibrium, so the Gibbs free energy change for fusion is zero: \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S = 0\), which gives \(T = \dfrac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}\). Converting the enthalpy of fusion to joules, \(\Delta H = 30.4\ kJ\ mol^{-1} = 30400\ J\ mol^{-1}\), while \(\Delta S = 28.4\ J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}\). Hence \(T = \dfrac{30400}{28.4} = 1070.4\) K, and to the nearest integer the melting point of sodium chloride is \(1070\) K.
authoredSolutions.82: The four distinct digits include \(7\) as the largest, the other three coming from \(\{0,1,\dots,6\}\). Since the first two digits and the last two have equal sum, the four digits split into two pairs of equal sum, one pair containing \(7\). Pairing \(7\) with \(x\) forces the remaining two digits to sum to \(7+x\); the number of valid pairs is \(3,2,2,1,1\) for \(x=0,1,2,3,4\), i.e. \(9\) digit-configurations. Each configuration gives \(2\times2\times2=8\) codes (which pair occupies the first two places, and the order within each pair), so the number of possible codes is \(9\times8=72\).
